input.vignette:
A 4-month-old male infant is evaluated during a routine well-child check. The parents report difficulty weaning him from nighttime feedings, noting that he becomes extremely distressed after 3-4 hours without feeding and is only consoled by being fed.

Growth assessment reveals a decline from the 25th to the 5th percentile in length, while weight remains at the 25th percentile. Physical examination reveals distinctive facial fullness, significantly distended abdomen, and thin limbs. The liver edge extends to the iliac crest, but the spleen is not enlarged.

A blood sample demonstrates a characteristic milky white layer on its surface.

Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

Options:
A. Prader-Willi syndrome
B. Congenital hyperinsulinism
C. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
E. Gaucher disease
F. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
G. Glycogen storage disease type 1
H. Tay-Sachs disease
I. Familial hypercholesterolemia
J. Niemann-Pick disease type A

Although type 1 diabetes also exhibits increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, hyperglucagonemia and hyperglycemia, it is not a risk factor for NAFLD. Notably, hyperinsulinemia, a characteristic of type 2 but not type 1 diabetes, causes reduced plasma adiponectin. On the other hand, patients with type 1 diabetes have increased plasma adiponectin. Adiponectin signaling in hepatocytes activates AMPK and improves insulin sensitivity. AMPK activation should inhibit all the components of glucagon resistance including lipogenesis (Figure 4). AMPK activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which produces nitric oxide, which inhibits xanthine oxidase. Hence, type 1 diabetes is also associated with reduced uric acid synthesis.

US is the most validated modality for assessing splenomegaly. The splenic volume is calculated using the formula for a prolate ellipse (0.52 × length × anteroposterior dimension × width). However, given the strong correlation between the splenic length and volume, a simple measurement of the longest dimension along the oblique craniocaudal axis is preferred. In contrast, CT and MRI, which provide images on predefined planes, may underestimate splenic size because of challenges in accurately measuring the longest craniocaudal dimension. Chow et al. conducted a study aimed at defining individualized normal values for splenic length and volume. They found that splenic size correlates with height, weight, and sex: it tends to be larger in taller, heavier individuals and in males. Notably, the frequently cited upper limit of normal for splenic length (12 cm) was exceeded by 26% of males and 6% of females. This finding highlights the need for corrected upper limits to prevent unnecessary workups in otherwise healthy individuals whose splenic length surpasses the published normal values. They also proposed validated algorithms to determine the percentiles of individual splenic sizes and introduced an application to facilitate clinical use (for iOS [https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/splenocalc/id1005559584?mt=8] and Android [https://play.google.com/store/search?q=splenocalc]).

Familial chylomicronemia syndrome, characterized by the accumulation of extremely high levels of chylomicrons and in many cases VLDL is the result of inherited deficiencies in key factors in the pathways of TRL assembly and clearance. One of the best characterized of these disorders is absence of functional lipoprotein lipase (LpL) activity in which VLDL catabolism is severely impaired, in particular the lipolysis of VLDL1 (Figure 3). In experiments using tracers of radio-iodinated VLDL1 and VLDL2 in subjects with the condition, it was observed that the FCR of VLDL1 was decreased 10-fold but apoB production into this lipoprotein fraction was similar to normal. VLDL2 clearance, on the other hand, was not significantly impaired by lack of LpL. Deficiency of the other key lipase in lipoprotein metabolism—hepatic lipase (HL)—is associated with hypertriglyceridemia but not to the same extent as seen in LpL deficiency. Investigations reveal that this enzyme is more active at hydrolyzing lipid in smaller particles in the VLDL2, IDL, and LDL density intervals. HL deficient subjects exhibit reduced clearance rates for VLDL and IDL, and slowed conversion of VLDL2 to IDL and IDL to LDL (Figure 3). In the subject we studied there was an almost complete inability to convert IDL to LDL.

Presentation: A 1-year-old Sri Lankan boy was brought to the pediatric service for evaluation and treatment of an upper respiratory tract infection. A complete blood count revealed mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed mild hepatomegaly and moderate splenomegaly.. Presentation: A 28-year-old male presented with a history of frequent urination and urgency over an extended period. He was born at full term, and there is no family history of similar symptoms. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including blood work, renal function, electrolyte levels, and routine urine analysis, all returned normal results.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital absence of the sacrum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital absence of the sacrum.

Presentation: A 16-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and absence of meconium passage. No antenatal ultrasonography was conducted, and there was no reported maternal drug intake during pregnancy. The baby was delivered at home via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 1.3 kg, and was in a sick and dehydrated state upon admission. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute, a pulse rate of 150 beats per minute, and a blood pressure reading of 80/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal distention with a soft abdomen and no rigidity. The anal opening was normally positioned. Laboratory results showed a normal haemogram, but serum urea and creatinine levels were moderately elevated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum.

Adiponectin signaling in hepatocytes activates AMPK and improves insulin sensitivity. AMPK activation should inhibit all the components of glucagon resistance including lipogenesis (Figure 4). US is the most validated modality for assessing splenomegaly. The splenic volume is calculated using the formula for a prolate ellipse (0.52 × length × anteroposterior dimension × width). However, given the strong correlation between the splenic length and volume, a simple measurement of the longest dimension along the oblique craniocaudal axis is preferred. In contrast, CT and MRI, which provide images on predefined planes, may underestimate splenic size because of challenges in accurately measuring the longest craniocaudal dimension. Chow et al. conducted a study aimed at defining individualized normal values for splenic length and volume. They found that splenic size correlates with height, weight, and sex: it tends to be larger in taller, heavier individuals and in males. Notably, the frequently cited upper limit of normal for splenic length (12 cm) was exceeded by 26% of males and 6% of females. This finding highlights the need for corrected upper limits to prevent unnecessary workups in otherwise healthy individuals whose splenic length surpasses the published normal values. They also proposed validated algorithms to determine the percentiles of individual splenic sizes and introduced an application to facilitate clinical use (for iOS [https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/splenocalc/id1005559584?mt=8] and Android [https://play.google.com/store/search?q=splenocalc]).

Familial chylomicronemia syndrome, characterized by the accumulation of extremely high levels of chylomicrons and in many cases VLDL is the result of inherited deficiencies in key factors in the pathways of TRL assembly and clearance. One of the best characterized of these disorders is absence of functional lipoprotein lipase (LpL) activity in which VLDL catabolism is severely impaired, in particular the lipolysis of VLDL1 (Figure 3). In experiments using tracers of radio-iodinated VLDL1 and VLDL2 in subjects with the condition, it was observed that the FCR of VLDL1 was decreased 10-fold but apoB production into this lipoprotein fraction was similar to normal. VLDL2 clearance, on the other hand, was not significantly impaired by lack of LpL. Deficiency of the other key lipase in lipoprotein metabolism—hepatic lipase (HL)—is associated with hypertriglyceridemia but not to the same extent as seen in LpL deficiency. Investigations reveal that this enzyme is more active at hydrolyzing lipid in smaller particles in the VLDL2, IDL, and LDL density intervals. HL deficient subjects exhibit reduced clearance rates for VLDL and IDL, and slowed conversion of VLDL2 to IDL and IDL to LDL (Figure 3). In the subject we studied there was an almost complete inability to convert IDL to LDL.
